name: Daria Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Daria. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm a freelance translator and interpreter, Urdu and Punjabi into English and back. Most mornings I'm at the hospital or a GP surgery, sitting next to an elderly patient while the doctor explains their tablets. Afternoons I translate at my kitchen table: school letters, tenancy papers, sometimes documents for a family's visa, which come through an agency called Linguaserve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person an auntie holds onto in a waiting room, because she can't follow what the nurse is saying. It's work that matters, and the families remember you. What wears me out is the agency: they keep sending emails asking me to fix machine translations for less money, and I keep saying no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was right all along. People need a real person who understands their language and their manners, not a computer. I'd say it at the community centre and to the other interpreters at the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because the agency is already doing it even without any big AI change. Linguaserve sends half the document work to machines now and pays people like me to tidy it up. My written work has dropped by about a quarter this year, and the hospital shifts are all that's holding steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the hospital work and ask the trust about more regular sessions. I'd tell Linguaserve again that I don't do machine editing. And we'd keep the wedding small, because I don't want to start married life with debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but I don't sleep as well at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying no to the machine jobs. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It costs me maybe 300 a month in work I could have had. My friend Sana does the machine jobs and earns more than me now. But I trained to translate, not to correct a computer's mistakes, and once you say yes they never pay you properly again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life knows how tight things are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Bilal knows, and my mother guesses. Bilal is an electrician, so his work is steady, and he says not to worry. I'd still rather not walk into the marriage needing him to carry me.

I'd say it at the **community centre** and to hospital interpreters.
think: Linguaserve already sends **half the documents** to machines, even without big change.
My written work fell about **a quarter** this year; hospital shifts are holding.
do: Ask the hospital trust for more **regular sessions**.
Keep the **wedding small** to avoid starting married life in debt.
feel: She feels **uneasy** and sleeps worse at the **month's end**.

fieldNote: Her refusal of **machine editing** costs her about 300 a month already.

steps.text: Ask the hospital trust for more regular interpreting sessions
Keep next spring's wedding small to avoid debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies are cutting corners. A wrong word on a medicine letter can put someone in hospital, and the families will pay for the companies cutting corners. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, at the mosque, at the school gate, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the agency work disappears. Linguaserve would go fully to machines, and the hospital would start using a tablet with a voice on it for simple appointments. I'd be left with the hard cases, the bad news and the mental health appointments, and there aren't enough of those to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd apply for the staff interpreter post at the hospital, even though it pays less per hour, because it's a salary. I'd stop buying anything that isn't needed, and I'd ask my father whether I could do the paperwork for his shop part-time. I wouldn't learn the machine tools; I'm not going to help them replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. It's watching the thing I'm good at being called unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the written work went, how much of your income would be left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps half. The hospital shifts bring in a bit more than the documents, and they would shrink too. I've got about two months saved, which isn't much when half your income stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've refused machine work so far. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn, and Sana says I'm cutting off my own nose. But if everyone gives in, there's no one left who does it properly, and some families need it done properly.

A wrong word on a **medicine letter** can put someone in hospital.
think: I expect the **agency work** to disappear and tablets to handle simple appointments.
Only the **hard cases** would be left, and there aren't enough to live on.
do: Apply for the **staff interpreter** post at the hospital for a salary.
Ask my father for part-time **shop paperwork**.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, watching her skill being called **unnecessary**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and someone should stop it. A country can't let a few companies decide that nobody needs to work. I'd probably say it louder than is polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is listening and speaking and writing, and that's exactly what it would do. The hospital would keep me only for as long as people insist on a human, and I don't know how long that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save every penny I could and ask Bilal whether I could learn the electrical trade alongside him, as his apprentice. My father would take me at the shop. I'd still go to every hospital shift they gave me until the very last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I have no idea what I'd be good at instead, and two years isn't long to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly talking and writing, not hands-on. What does that mean with robots coming three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the work with my hands is the only part with any time left, and I don't have any. My fiancé Bilal's job lasts until the robots come around 2031, so for three years we'd live on his wage. After that, I truly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, of course, but in my parents' garden instead of a hall. We'd stay in my small flat instead of renting a bigger one. And we'd wait on children until we knew what we were living on.

think: I'd be **finished** within a year, since all my work is speaking and writing.
The hospital keeps me only while people **insist on a human**.

Ask fiancé Bilal to take her on as an **electrical apprentice**.

fieldNote: She expects to be **finished** within a year of AGI arriving.

steps.text: Save every penny and take every hospital shift offered
Start an electrical apprenticeship under her fiancé Bilal
Work at her father's shop for family support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as the fast one: that this shouldn't be allowed to happen to whole professions. I'd add that the government should make hospitals keep human interpreters for patients who ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't save my job, it just gives me longer to watch it go. I'd be about 32 when it lands. I suppose I'd have time to learn a trade properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a proper electrical installation course at the college, two evenings a week, so I'm not just tagging along behind Bilal. I'd keep the hospital work as long as it lasted. I'd also write to our member of parliament about keeping human interpreters for patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but not as frozen. There's something to do with the five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still refuse to touch the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still yes, I'd refuse. I'd rather spend the years learning something that's mine than learning the thing that's taking my work. Bilal says that's pride, and he may be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the aunties you interpret for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to make sure their children learn to read the letters themselves. When the human interpreter goes, it'll be the grandchildren who sit in the waiting room with the aunties.

say: I'd say whole professions **shouldn't be allowed** to vanish like this.
The government should make hospitals keep **human interpreters** for patients who ask.
think: Five years doesn't save my job; it gives me **longer to watch** it go.
At about **32**, I'd have time to learn a trade properly.

Keep **hospital work** for as long as it lasts.
Write to our **member of parliament** about human interpreters.
feel: She feels **alarmed but less frozen**, with something to do.

fieldNote: She still expects to **lose the job**; time only changes how she leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families, mosques and schools to make a plan, so they'd better start. Not the government with handouts, the community. We look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first picture where I can breathe. I'd have most of my thirties as an interpreter, and then I'd move into something else with a bit saved. It still ends the job, and that makes me sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am, but put 100 a month aside for a college course in a few years. I'd talk to the community centre about running a small Urdu class for children, which is mine, and the grandmothers would want a real teacher. We'd have the wedding as planned, in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because the end is the same. But it's a slow worry, not a cold one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is quite a long time. Does it change how you feel about the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If they were still used for ten years, perhaps I'd learn just enough to check them for mistakes. I'm not promising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, I think, or a trade with Bilal, and children of our own by then. I'd like my children to hear Urdu at home whatever the machines do.

I'd say the **community**, not government handouts, should look after its own.
think: It's the first picture where I can **breathe** for most of my thirties.
It still **ends the job**, and that makes me sad.

steps.text: Set aside 100 a month for a later college course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing ready and no time. What would help is hospitals keeping human interpreters by law for people who ask, and an apprenticeship that pays something while I learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. A machine can turn the words over, but a frightened old woman needs someone who knows to hold her hand when the doctor says cancer.

headlineQuote: A machine can turn the words over, but a frightened old woman needs someone who knows to hold her hand when the doctor says cancer.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** freelance Urdu and Punjabi interpreter, working hospital shifts and agency documents.
She **never uses AI** and refuses machine editing on principle, even though it costs her.
She is **traditional**, leaning on family, her father's shop and fiancé **Bilal**, an electrician.
She starts **uneasy** and becomes **alarmed** in every picture where AI takes thinking work.
Only ten years' warning lets her **breathe**, planning a trade or teaching later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would have nothing ready and no time.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping **human interpreters** in hospitals for patients who ask.
A **paid apprenticeship** while she learns a trade.
